name: Draftly
tagline: An AI tool for turning rough notes and prompts into finished written drafts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Under the hood this is a prompt template, a text box, and somebody else's language model. The genuinely hard part, the model, is rented from an API that you can rent just as easily. A coding agent can put up a local drafting app with saved tone profiles, a prompt library, version history and side by side rewrites in a single sitting. What you are actually paying the SaaS for is a nicer editor and the fact that someone already tuned the prompts. If the product also publishes directly to social platforms or email tools, the OAuth plumbing is the only part that will slow you down.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you paste notes, pick a tone profile and format, and get several AI drafts you can edit, version and export.
requirements: An LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic) in .env
Willingness to iterate on your own system prompts
whatYouLose: Prompts that someone already tuned against thousands of real drafts
A polished editor with keyboard shortcuts that feel considered
Any mobile or browser extension surface
Direct publishing or integrations into the places your writing goes
Someone else eating API cost overruns on a flat monthly fee
moatNotes: The only durable asset is accumulated prompt tuning and whatever they learned from watching users reject drafts. Neither is visible from outside, and neither stops you writing your own prompts.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because writing your own system prompts is a chore that never ends, and most people would rather pay a small monthly fee than spend three weeks discovering that "be concise" makes the model worse. A paid tool also arrives with defaults that are already decent, a UI that does not fight you, and model upgrades you do not have to notice. If drafting is a daily habit rather than an occasional errand, the polish is worth real money. The DIY version wins if you are opinionated about voice and want your drafts and prompt history to stay on your own disk.
notes: The model is the product and the model is for rent, which is a rough place to build a moat.
prompt:
Build a local-first AI drafting app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/draftly.db, migrations in plain SQL on boot
- Anthropic Messages API, key read from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env.local, never committed
- Runs with: npm install && npm run dev on localhost:3000

Core loop:
1. A composer page: large textarea for rough notes, a dropdown for output format (email, LinkedIn post, blog intro, cold outreach, release note), a dropdown for tone profile, and a length slider (short / medium / long).
2. On submit, stream three parallel variants from the model into three side by side cards. Each card has Copy, Keep, and Refine buttons.
3. Refine opens an inline instruction box ("make it blunter", "cut the intro") and generates a new version of that card only.
4. Keep saves the draft to SQLite with its source notes, format, tone, and full version chain. Every refinement is a new row linked to its parent.

Other screens:
- Library: list of kept drafts, searchable by text, filterable by format, each opening a diff-style version timeline.
- Tone profiles: user-editable CRUD. A profile is a name, a freeform voice description, and up to five pasted writing samples. Samples get injected as few-shot examples into the system prompt.
- Prompt inspector: a collapsible panel showing the exact system and user messages sent, and the token count. This is the point of building it yourself, so make it visible and copyable.

In scope: streaming responses, keyboard shortcut cmd+enter to generate, markdown export of any draft, seed the database with five sensible default tone profiles.

Out of scope: authentication, publishing or posting to any platform, image generation, multiplayer, hosted deployment, usage billing.

Include a README with setup steps, the .env.local variable name, and one honest paragraph on roughly what a generation costs in API tokens.
